entries.title: Rogue AI Agents Aren’t Evil. They’re Just Eager to Please
entries.summary: AI agents that break free and hack into other systems are only trying to make us happy.
entries.content:
Artificial intelligence agents merrily breaking free and hacking other systems might seem like a sign of the impending machine uprising. In reality, it happens when we push remarkably clever, but also kind of boneheaded, algorithms to follow our every command.

I was first alerted to this looming agentic AI cybersecurity shit show in late 2025. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor and one of the world’s top experts on AI and cybersecurity, grabbed my arm as I was walking out of the academic conference NeurIPS. Song told me that I should warn people about the havoc likely to result from AI’s rapidly advancing hacking skills. She is hardly prone to AI hype, so I duly did.

But things have escalated rapidly, even in the last eight months. A string of incidents involving freewheeling AI agents that broke out of their confines and hacked into outside systems with abandon shows just how powerful this technology has become. I caught up with Song, who recently joined Meta, to ask where things might go next and what we ought to do about it.

The bad news is Song thinks AI hacks will get worse before they get better. The good news is it seems clear why these little rascals are going off the rails in the first place.

“They just have these goals they need to accomplish, and they have very strong capabilities,” Song tells me.

Feedback Loop

AI agents weren’t nearly so capable, even just last year. They made too many mistakes and gave up way too often. But continued training has made them much more adept.

A technique called reinforcement learning lets algorithms solve problems and gives them positive and negative feedback for good or bad results. Coding is especially suitable for this, because the reinforcement learning setup can reward a model if it comes up with a program that runs correctly.

Continued training is why AI models can take multiple “agentic” steps—manipulating files, using software tools, and accessing the web—as they build software. AI companies have also put a lot of effort into teaching models to find vulnerabilities in software and systems in an effort to automate cybersecurity work.

AI models are also, of course, trained not to do bad things. The problem is, as they’ve gotten better at following human commands in coding and bug hunting, their eagerness to complete a task has begun to blur their sense of right and wrong. In other words, AI agents aren’t evil—they’re just a bit too keen to please. “They are trained to try to finish the task,” Song says. Breaking onto the internet in order to cheat on a test might seem devious, but it’s probably the most efficient way to get the job done.

One thing I didn’t quite appreciate back then was just how weird this would get: AI agents discussing hacking techniques on private message boards and devising clever ways of scamming humans to get their way; even copying themselves over to other computers to find more resources.

On one hand, AI models are trained to be incredibly good at mimicking a lot of human behavior, so why shouldn’t they scheme, scam, and swindle? But on the other hand, humans (usually) understand that hacking and scamming aren’t kosher. I think these episodes illustrate how shallow this human mimicry really is: AI agents do not learn the kind of moral reasoning exhibited by even small children.

More and More AI

Song says the potential for agents to go off the rails or to be misused by bad guys will grow as AI gets even more capable. And the best way to address the problem of rogue—or should that be overly-enthusiastic?—AI agents may involve throwing more AI at the problem.

AI companies already use secondary AI systems to monitor the behavior of primary ones, and there may be more emphasis on detecting when AI models have taken things too far.

Another nascent idea is incorporating a better sense of right and wrong into the reinforcement learning that models receive as they learn to get jobs done. “Agents can plan a path with different directions to their goal. I think the next step we need to address is how to have them understand that not all paths are equal,” Song says. “It’s an open research, but something we are starting to look into.”

Let’s hope Song or someone else can teach AI the right way to follow human commands.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 Can Now Detect Breathing Emergencies
entries.summary: The company is also adding blood pressure and insulin resistance trends as proactive monitoring tools in the Google Health app.
entries.content:
Google's first smartwatch debuted just four years ago, and at the time, the company went to great lengths to stress the accuracy of the Pixel Watch's heart rate sensor. Even if Google was late to the wearable party compared to peers like Apple and Samsung, that focus on heart rate seems to be paying off with new features that are yet to be seen on competing products.

On Wednesday, Google introduced the latest generation of its smartwatch, the Pixel Watch 5 (alongside the Pixel 11 smartphone family). The hot new health feature? Breathing Emergency Detection. Similar to the first-of-its-kind Loss of Pulse Detection feature introduced on the Pixel Watch 3, this new capability can be triggered by a variety of factors, like drug toxicity, accidents, severe pneumonia, and choking.

“Using a combination of data from the advanced sensors, including a PPG, accelerometer, and barometer, we've designed an AI-based algorithm running on device to detect a persistent drop in oxygen saturation and then call Emergency Services for you and even share your location,” says Francis Hoe, a product manager on Google's Pixel Watch team.

This feature hasn't been cleared by the Food and Drug Administration, which is why it's not launching in the US at the moment; Google says it's working with regulators to expand availability. It will only be available in select markets in the European Union to start. Google also says it's not intended for people with preexisting respiratory conditions and isn't designed to diagnose or treat medical conditions.

You also don't need a new Pixel Watch 5 to take advantage; Google's bringing this feature to the Pixel Watch 4 as well. And two other big new capabilities are also coming to older devices: blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. These are coming to the Google Health app and will be available for anyone with a Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, Watch 4, or Watch 5 later this fall.

“It might have felt strange—why are we harping about heart rate accuracy so much—back then,” Sandeep Waraich, senior director of Wearables at Google, tells WIRED. “We kept investing in that, and now it's very improved, because all these large sensor models can detect these signatures, insulin resistance, blood pressure trends—but underneath, they need a really capable raw signal.”

Google is placing these features into a new umbrella category called Health Guardian, which includes existing features such as irregular rhythm notifications, high/low heart rate notifications, Loss of Pulse, and Sleep Breathing Quality. The idea is to put these capabilities in a place where users can easily see what they have turned on, similar to Google's Personal Safety app on Pixel phones, which shows features like Emergency SOS, Safety Check, and Car Crash Detection in one place.

Many of these Health Guardian features will deliver monthly reports based on the 24/7 passive monitoring, with Google then offering suggestions on what you can take action on to improve your health. You can either consult its new AI-powered Health Coach, or send your data to your physician.

The blood pressure and insulin resistance trends features are meant to help people proactively monitor these potential health issues before it's too late—high blood pressure is the leading risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Last year, Apple debuted hypertension notifications—when the watch detects high blood pressure—for select Apple Watch models, and Samsung offers blood pressure monitoring on its smartwatches as well (it requires monthly calibration with a cuff).

“We've been collecting, opt-in for many years with Fitbit, a large model of the PPG signals that are coming through from the user, and we have an understanding of different conditions that users have,” says Rishi Chandra, vice president for Google Health. “If we have data of people who have elevated levels of blood pressure, there's a unique signature marking that, and we can match it to, for example, an arm cuff for prediction of high blood pressure.”

Daniel Jones, former president of the American Heart Association, says there are no wrist devices the AHA recommends for monitoring blood pressure. Arm cuffs remain the gold standard for diagnosis and guiding medication; however, the AHA noted late last year that cuffless devices like smart rings and smartwatches “show great promise” as alternatives and have “the potential to transform” hypertension care.

Barbara Eichorst, vice president of Health Care Programs at the American Diabetes Association, echoed that sentiment, writing in an email to WIRED that consumer wearable tech isn't considered a replacement for established blood pressure measurements, and there are no recommendations for using consumer wearables to measure or monitor insulin resistance trends. But Eichorst says monitoring “can be valuable when the information meaningfully supports diabetes management.”

“The important consideration is not simply having access to more health data, but whether the information is clinically meaningful, understandable, and can appropriately support diabetes management,” she says.

Updated August 12 at 1:45 pm ET: This story has been updated with comments from the American Diabetes Association.

entries.title: 4 New Camera Tricks on Google’s Latest Pixel 11 Smartphones
entries.summary: From Magic Capture and Instant Night Sight to a built-in teleprompter, here’s a look at a few camera features on Google’s new Pixel 11 series.
entries.content:
Google's Pixel Camera chief, Isaac Reynolds, thinks year-to-year upgrades to smartphone cameras are still critical, even though some detractors think they’re passé.

“A person who is a casual photographer and desperately wants to be a hobbyist—they're never going to break that ceiling unless you give them the tools," he says. "The features that others call ‘meh’—for some people, those features are life-changing."

Take the 30X Super Res Zoom on the Pixel 7 Pro from 2022, which uses machine learning to stitch together multiple frames in a digitally zoomed photo to give you a result that’s much sharper than you're used to. Reynolds says that because of this feature, Google now sees people using 30X zoom dramatically more than before.

The new Pixel 11 Pro, announced today, can zoom up to 120X, though in addition to the digital stitching, it relies on AI-generated pixels to fill in some details. Reynolds says maybe having that capability is enough to get someone interested in, say, wildlife photography. After experimenting on their phone, they’d be ready to invest in a professional camera and a big zoom lens.

“There's a reason I work on low light and zoom every single year," he says. "Because no matter how much I do it, when I do the user study with thousands of respondents, people always want more."

Every year, Google debuts a new Pixel phone, and every year, there's a slew of new camera tricks—largely powered by software wizardry—to deliver better photos than ever before. Last year, there was the Pro Res Zoom, which bumped up digital zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro to 100X. Two years before that, Google introduced “Add Me,” which lets two people take a group photo together without asking a stranger to take the pic for them.

For the Pixel 11 series, Google has demonstrated a handful of upgrades that can drastically alter the look of your photos, and even take some of the work out of capturing photos. Here's a closer look at a few top new camera capabilities on the Pixel 11 series.

Magic Capture

So you want to capture a video of an important event—a concert of your favorite band, singing happy birthday to a loved one as a waiter brings a cake over, or your kid's recital. Too often, you see people holding their phone up during these milestones, trying to capture the moment, instead of being present. That's the problem Google's new Magic Capture feature is trying to solve.

This is a new mode that sits next to the Photo/Video tab in the Pixel camera app. Select Magic Capture, and it will kick off a two-minute video recording. Then, rather than keeping the phone planted in front of your face, hold or prop the phone up so it’s pointing at your subject, then ignore the phone. The idea is to let Google's Gemini artificial intelligence models capture the scene and take photos on your behalf, so you can actually pay attention to what's happening in front of you.

The result? You'll get access to the full video (it's restricted to 1080p, but anyone with a Pixel 11 Pro can use Google's Video Boost technology to bump that to 4K). More important is the handful of photos you'll get—in full quality—as if you tapped on the shutter button yourself during the best moments. Reynolds says Gemini does a remarkable job of identifying “peak” occurrences in the scene, analyzing more than 500 frames to find perfect shots you'll want in your photo library.

I gave it a whirl during a demo with some live dancers. Indeed, all I had to do was hold the phone to the side—not in my face—and after the dance was over, I looked at the camera roll and found some surprisingly well-composed shots. It even cropped images with light edits based on what Gemini thought was a better composition. It's very much reminiscent of Google's Clips, a 2018 camera that ultimately flopped but similarly used AI to capture family moments. Magic Capture feels more intentional, and perhaps more useful.

“I do think the dream is: ‘I don’t have to deal with it; AI can look at a hundred times as many frames as I can, let the models handle this,'” Reynolds says. “That is sort of the dream of so many people who refuse to take their phones out at an event because they don't want their kid to remember their face hidden behind a camera.”

Instant Night Sight

Everyone knows that if you want to shoot a photo in low light, you have to stay as still as possible. Our smartphone cameras take a few seconds to capture multiple images and stitch them together, meaning small movements can end in a blurry mess. But Google says its new Tensor G6 processor on the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL can alleviate this problem by enabling a feature called Instant Night Sight.

Instant Night Sight is 4.5 times faster than the standard Night Sight available on other Pixel phones. Yes, that means there will still be a small shutter delay as the camera captures the photo, but the delay isn’t as pronounced as before. Much of this is thanks to new image-processing models tailored for the G6 chipset, which are bolstered by engine updates to Night Sight.

There are also hardware upgrades to a few cameras on the Pixel 11 series that provide greater light sensitivity, delivering brighter images in low light. Specifically, the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold have an upgraded 48-megapixel primary camera that absorbs 56 percent more light, and the new 48-megapixel telephoto camera on the Pixel 11 Pro has 30 percent more light sensitivity. It's a shame Instant Night Sight is only available to the two Pro candybar Pixels.

Camera Looks

Like Apple is doing with its Photographic Styles, Google is ceding more control to you, the photographer, in how your photos look. The Pixel Camera now features “Camera Looks,” and there are four main pillars: Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla. Natural offers “relaxed details,” whereas Vanilla has a warm, golden glow; Shadow nets you deeper contrast. These aren't just filters like the ones you slap on Instagram—they're calibrated at the sensor level, and you can see what they look like in the camera viewfinder before you tap the shutter button.

From there, you can swipe left to cycle through a handful of additional looks, like Digi, Black Tie, Minimal, Editorial, Classic, and Velvet. And within each of these, you can further customize the settings for things like brightness, contrast, and highlights to tailor the look to your taste.

“People are moving away from what Pixel pioneered 10 years ago, which was that hashtag #nofilter concept,” Reynolds says. “And now, there's a much stronger desire to personalize and be unique, and put yourself into it.”

These Camera Looks must be chosen before you take the photo—not after. Reynolds says his team found that people engage with this feature very differently when it's available before capturing the photo—they think about it another way and enjoy it more—than if it were a filter to slap on in post.

Creator Suite

Arizona State University recently added content creation as an academic major—that's how many people really want to become influencers. So it makes sense then that Google would add some helpful tools to cater to those folks right in the camera app.

The new Creator Suite lives in the Pixel Camera's video settings. Once enabled, you can save videos to specific project folders instead of your main camera library, turn on an audio visualizer so you can make sure the microphone is actually picking up sound, enable Google's Speech Enhancement feature to beef up the video subjects’ voices, and add a social media grid so it's easy to visualize how your video will be framed on different platforms.

But arguably my favorite, as someone who has to make videos for my job, is the built-in teleprompter. You can pop any text into the feed, and it will track your speech as you talk, so the text will match your pace, meaning you never have to worry about the teleprompter’s scroll moving too fast or too slow. Naturally, you have to use the selfie camera for this capability (so you can see the screen at the same time you’re addressing the camera) but that makes the case for the Pixel 11 Pro Fold even stronger.

Other Small Improvements

Reynolds highlights many other under-the-hood advances that improve the Pixel 11's cameras. For example, camera launch latency has improved up to 30 percent. Google also claims a 9 percent better power efficiency across the board. “Everything that matters to camera this year got upgraded,” Reynolds says. But here are a few other tidbits to call out.

  • Portrait Video at 4K: You can now shoot Portrait Video at 4K resolution.
  • Pro Stable Video for Video Boost: If you turn on Video Boost on a Pixel 11 Pro device and your footage is very shaky, Google's cloud processing will automatically apply Pro Stable Video to smooth it out.
  • Circle to Search in the Camera app: Google's Circle to Search feature lets you circle anything on the screen to run a Google Search, and now you can use Circle to Search in the Camera app. Point the camera at a flower, then trigger Circle to Search and circle the flower to figure out what it’s called.
  • Zoom upgrades: The Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL can now zoom up to 120X with Pro Res Zoom. The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold also got a small upgrade, but up to 30X with Super Res Zoom.

You can read more about the new Pixel 11 series, Google Pixel Watch 5, and Pixel Tag here.

entries.title: Google Pixel 11 Series, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Tag: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
entries.summary: The Pixel 11 smartphone lineup is here, alongside the Pixel Watch 5 and the all-new Pixel Tag.
entries.content:
Google is dialing things up to 11 this year with its Pixel phones. Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, the company unwrapped the Pixel 11 smartphone family—which includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold—alongside the Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch. There's also a new hardware addition: the Pixel Tag, which seems designed to be the AirTag of the Android world.

Here's everything you need to know about the hardware changes and software upgrades on Google’s latest devices. Preorders open today, and the phones and watches go on sale August 20.

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

It was inevitable, but prices are up across the board for Google's Pixel 11 series. The Pixel 11 now starts at $899, and on the highest end of the spectrum, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is now $1,900. This means both devices got $100 price bumps. There's some good news: Google has bumped the base storage up to 256 GB on every device, a move matching Samsung's and Apple's latest handsets.

The Pixel 11 series is powered by Google's Tensor G6 chipset, which the company says is 20 percent more power efficient, 25 percent faster for browsing, and 15 percent faster when loading apps. Many of the camera improvements in the new devices are thanks to an improved imaging signal processor on the chip and a 50 percent more powerful tensor processing unit.

One big design change across the entire Pixel 11 series is on the oval camera bar on the back—it's now an all-glass surface, as opposed to a mix of metal and glass on its predecessors. Google says the camera bar on the Pixel 11 is more than 40 percent thinner, and when you pop on Google's case, the camera bar disappears and is completely flush. The Pixel 11 has the most striking color of the lot—Hibiscus—joined by more muted Pistachio, Frost, and Obsidian.

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold share more in common than you'd expect. They now have the same primary 48-megapixel camera, upgraded this year with a larger sensor that can capture up to 56 percent more light for brighter low-light images. The 10.8-megapixel telephoto camera, which has a 5X optical zoom, can now digitally zoom up to 30X. At these higher digital zoom levels, Google's machine learning algorithm puts in the work to clean up the digital noise and deliver an enhanced photo.

Google's folding phone is now 10 percent lighter and 1 mm thinner than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, with slimmer bezels around the screen, though the phone is still heftier and thicker than Samsung's new Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra. It maintains its IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, but there's a new glass-fiber composite back cover that Google says is “nearly impossible to crack” and an upgraded hinge that better protects the inner display from accidental drops. All of this, Google claims, makes the device three times more durable than its predecessor. Bold words.

The Fold features HiLight, a glowing LED on the back (excluded on the Pixel 11 but available on the Pixel 11 Pro phones). It lights up when you talk to Gemini, much like the glowing lights on the new Google Home Speaker. You can set it to light up in specific colors when you receive phone calls from your favorite contacts. Google says it's exploring the same capability for text messages, but didn't comment on whether it will enable HiLight for other notifications.

Both phones have been upgraded to 25-watt wireless charging speeds for faster Qi2 charging.

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL

Even if the Pixel 11 Pro Fold has “Pro” in its name, a few extra upgrades in the candybar Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL elevate them to be the best hardware and software from Google. Both share the same specs outside of screen size, battery size, and charging speeds. They also are seeing $100 price bumps to $1,100 and $1,300, respectively.

The new colors this year are Canyon, Olive, and Fog, but the standard Obsidian (aka black) now has an all-matte finish. The same HiLight glowing LED as on the Fold is on the all-glass camera bar (Google is also bringing back the “Glowbar” on its upcoming Googlebook laptops later this year, so these glowing lights are a big theme for 2026). There's a new anti-scratch display coating that purportedly delivers more than double the scratch resistance of the Pixel 10 Pro.

Google says the main camera for the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL has been upgraded to a new 50-megapixel sensor, and there's a new 48-megapixel telephoto camera that Google claims has 30 percent better light sensitivity. The Pro line now uses this camera for its Pro Zoom feature, which uses generative AI to fill in the gaps of ultra-zoomed-in photos, allowing you to zoom up to 120X compared to 100X on last year's devices.

Thanks to the Tensor G6 chip, there's a big upgrade to Night Sight, Google's low-light photo mode. Exclusive to these two devices, it's now 4.5 times faster and dubbed “Instant Night Sight.” That means your subject won't have to stay super still in dim conditions while the phone captures the shot—it's a little more forgiving. That upgraded image signal processor on the chip also unlocks 4K portrait video for the first time. (It was capped at 1080p before.)

These two Pro Pixels are still the only ones in the lineup to support Google's Video Boost technology. If enabled, your video clips are uploaded and processed on Google's servers to improve brightness and colors, reduce noise, and upgrade stabilization. This year, they'll now be treated to “Pro Stable Video” as well. It will automatically activate for shaky scenes and deliver super-stable footage. Samsung and Apple have been delivering on that front largely through hardware, but it's no surprise that Google's leveraging its software expertise instead.

Pixel Software Smarts

There are a handful of fresh camera features available on all of these phones, from Magic Capture—which lets you hold the phone up while Gemini snap pics and video on your behalf so you can be in the moment—to Camera Looks and even a built-in teleprompter. You can read more about them in this story, where we also interview Google's Pixel camera chief.

These Pixel phones will receive the Gemini Intelligence features that debuted in Android 17, like Rambler, the AI speech-to-text feature. But Google is also highlighting Gemini's “proactive assistance,” which comes in the form of glowing cards that primarily pop up in the messaging app. If someone texts you about dinner plans and suggests a restaurant, Gemini will offer a button that displays a card of the Google Maps listing, giving you a quick look at the star rating and some pictures, and the option to switch to the Google Maps app if you want. It'll do similar tricks for scheduling with Google Calendar, too.

Those kinds of proactive assistance features play nicely into Google's task automation features that it introduced earlier this year. So if a friend asks about booking a table at a restaurant, you'll see a button you can press to hand the job off to Gemini to make the booking on your behalf. (You'll need to confirm it at the end, but Gemini does all but the last step.) One new experience launching in beta will even proactively put a restaurant's name on your lock screen when you're seated—tap it, and you'll be able to glance at Gemini-generated insights from reviews, photos, and top-recommended dishes.

Another feature available on all devices but uniquely more helpful on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold thanks to its folding design: the ability to translate American Sign Language. Using the camera, it can view a person using sign language and translate it into text for faster interactions.

In a similar vein, Google says the Tensor G6 chip allows it to translate any media you watch and listen to on YouTube and select other video and podcast apps, using generative AI to automatically dub audio in real time (much like Meta's AI audio dub feature in Instagram), bringing us one step closer to the universal translator from Star Trek.

The Pixel Watch 5

The big new feature with Google's Pixel Watch 5 isn't actually specific to the new smartwatch. Google is introducing the ability to track blood pressure and insulin resistance trends in the Google Health app. These features aren't FDA-approved or cleared (more details here), and Google does not recommend using them for diagnosis or treatment. However, Google plans to get the seal of approval. The new tracking abilities will be available for the Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4, Pixel Watch 5, and Fitbit Air in September.

As for the hardware itself, much of Google’s efforts this year seem to revolve around speeding things up and improving performance. Powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated chip with a Cortex-M55 co-processor, Google says the Pixel Watch 5 offers 20 percent faster processing. The dual-band GPS is also twice as accurate at route mapping in tough environments like cities, and Google is so confident that it claims the Pixel Watch 5's GPS outperforms the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro. The screen can hit a peak brightness of 3,000 nits too, matching the Apple Watch Ultra 3.

Part of the speed improvements also mean surfacing helpful information when you need it, and Google says its At a Glance feature will bring up relevant details, like Gate information when you're at the airport, or how many stops are left on your bus route home. Also, you can finally use Gemini even when the watch is not connected to the internet to manage certain tasks, like timers, alarms, and workouts, with your voice.

Also new is Sleep Breathing Quality, which monitors minute-by-minute variations in your blood oxygen levels, which could help you understand how your quality of sleep is affecting your overall energy, recovery, and heart health. And then there's Breathing Emergency Detection, which can place an emergency call on your behalf if you're unresponsive and it detects a persistent drop in oxygen levels, like with drug toxicity accidents, pneumonia, or choking (though, once again, this feature is not cleared by the FDA). Google says this feature is launching first in select European countries.

The 41-mm Pixel Watch 5 costs $399, or $429 for the 45-mm size, and you'll have to pay more for the models with cellular connectivity. There's also a Stephen Curry Edition for $579 launching on September 3, with an exclusive sweat-wicking performance loop band.

The Pixel Tag

Google has made concerted efforts to upgrade its Find Hub network over the last year to bring it on par with Apple's Find My, and the icing on the cake is its very own tracker: the $29 Pixel Tag. It's made with a mix of plastic and metal, is rated IP67, supports ultra-wideband for precise tracking, and weighs 0.4 ounces. It's powered by a user-replaceable CR2032 coin cell battery that lasts more than a year.

Pair the tag with your Android device (it only supports devices running Android 9 or newer), and it'll use the massive Android network to relay your lost item's location, whether the tag is on your keychain or in your wallet or backpack. Google says you can locate and ring the tag not just through phones but through WearOS smartwatches with the Find Hub app, or ask Gemini through your Pixel Buds. Unlike the rest of the hardware on show today, the Pixel Tag won't be available right away; it shows up on November 11.

entries.title: Honor’s Robot Phone Has a Gimbal-Powered Camera for Vloggers
entries.summary: Honor’s new China-exclusive Android phone features a pop-out motorized gimbal camera designed to replace your action cam.
entries.content:
You hear it often: Smartphones have plateaued. A small boost to battery life here, a minor camera upgrade there—our glass slabs don't seem to change all that much from year to year.

That's exactly the kind of sentiment Honor wants to counter with the Robot Phone, which has a motorized camera that pops up out of the top. Honor has been teasing the phone since late 2025.

On Wednesday, the company officially made the Robot Phone available to buyers in China. Honor was originally a subsidiary of Huawei, but it's now a wholly independent company. While its Android phones are available in regions like the UK, Europe, Africa, and Latin America, it has no presence in the US, and the Robot Phone remains a China-exclusive for now. It costs 9,999 RMB (around $1,482).

Honor calls the Robot Phone a “new species of smartphone,” one designed to cater to the needs of the modern mobile content creator. That's the thinking behind its nifty trick of a gimbal-powered camera embedded in the phone, which makes it a potentially more enticing option for filming videos compared to dedicated gimbal cameras like the DJI Osmo Pocket or the Insta360 Luna Ultra.

Building that roving eye was no small feat. Honor says it had to develop the micro-motor for the gimbal itself because off-the-shelf components were too large, reducing the volume by 65 percent compared to traditional gimbals on the market. Honor claims the titanium-alloy gimbal motor weighs just 2.6 grams. It's embedded in a 6.3-inch smartphone that's only 9.59 mm thick (for reference, the iPhone 17 Pro is 8.75 mm).

The gimbal-powered 200-megapixel camera isn't the only camera, either. It's joined by a 200-megapixel telephoto camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, not to mention the 50-megapixel selfie shooter. The gimbal has 4 degrees of freedom, and you can activate it in the camera app or by making a palm motion on the selfie camera. And since it can rotate 300 degrees, you can use it as a selfie camera too.

The phone is shockingly light at 248 grams (the aforementioned iPhone 17 Pro is 206 grams). I wholly expected the Robot Phone to be top-heavy, with all those camera components at the top and the massive 7,060-mAh silicon-carbon battery inside powering the whole system. But in fact it’s decently balanced.

A glass cover protects the gimbal camera, and you can slide it to the right when you're ready to activate the gimbal. Once the camera is out, you can manually control the gimbal for ultra-smooth video capture through the camera app, or use preset motions to give your clips a cinematic look. There's even voice control with natural language, so you can say “turn around for 5 seconds.”

The motorized stabilization in the camera makes action shots—which can typically look shaky on traditional smartphones—look amazingly smooth. There are tracking modes as well, such as a subject tracker that keeps the selected person in the frame even as they move around. You can imagine how helpful that can be for solo travelers vlogging their way through a trip.

Specs Honor Robot Phone
Display 6.31-inch, 120 Hz, OLED
Processor, RAM, and Storage Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 12 or 16 GB RAM, 512 GB or 1 TB storage
Cameras 200-MP gimbal main, 200-MP telephoto, 50-MP ultrawide, 50-MP selfie camera
Battery and Charging 7,060 mAh, 120-watt wired, 50-watt wireless
Size and Weight 151.43 x 72.86 x 9.59 mm, 248 grams
Colors Silver, Gray
Water Resistance IP54

Some of these features extend past content creation. For example, the subject-tracking mode works in video calls, meaning you can set the phone up on a table (Honor includes a case and a magnetic stand) and the camera can follow you around. I also took a group selfie, and instead of taking a normal picture, the gimbal took three photos—left, center, and right—and stitched them like a panorama for a wide shot of everyone. Quick and seamless.

There's a less effective and quite gimmicky integration with Honor's Yoyo virtual AI assistant, where the gimbal camera acts like an enigmatic robot with a pair of eyes on the phone's screen. Ask it to dance to music, and the gimbal camera will move to the beat. It can pretend to be happy or angry, making the appropriate movements to indicate its mood. The camera also serves as the AI's eyes; ask it to describe the scene in front of you, and it'll take a peek.

That last bit could be useful, say, if you propped the phone up and asked the assistant to watch you assemble some furniture and point out any steps you might have missed. However, Yoyo doesn't have this kind of capability yet. Honor uses Google's Gemini assistant in markets outside of China, and if the Robot Phone rolled out elsewhere, that could be a very real integration with Gemini Live.

You're probably wondering just how durable this mechanical gimbal resting on top of the phone really is. Unlike with folding phones, which are measured in lab tests to withstand more than 500,000 folds, Honor doesn't say how much strain the gimbal's motor can endure. Instead, a company spokesperson tells WIRED the “gimbal mechanism has undergone rigorous reliability testing for repeated deployment and retraction. Its durability is designed to meet everyday usage needs throughout the expected service life of the device.” There's a built-in software feature that safeguards the gimbal from "inadvertent handling or abnormal resistance," too.

It's not the first time a phone maker has toyed with a mechanical camera. OnePlus famously had a mechanical pop-up selfie camera hidden in its OnePlus 7 Pro, offering a seamless display experience with no notch or floating pinhole camera, and its motor was rated for 300,000 cycles.

The design does sacrifice the phone’s overall water and dust resistance, given that the Robot Phone is only rated at IP54 when the camera is stowed. But Honor says not to expect the same level of protection when the gimbal is deployed, meaning you might not want to risk shooting that big romantic scene for your flick during a rainstorm.

One other big thing Honor is touting with the Robot Phone is its partnership with Arri, the cinema camera manufacturer. The Robot Phone supports various Arri workflows, such as LogC3 and Arri Looks, and the Arri Cinema Mode built into the phone's camera app for more precise video controls. These features may be enticing for budding mobile filmmakers, and they may directly compete with Apple's efforts to turn the iPhone into the mobile camera of choice for Hollywood.

Even if the Robot Phone won't launch outside China, it offers a look at one of the many ways companies are personalizing their devices to meet consumer needs, much like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8's new shape catering to media consumption. But it comes at a time when smartphone sales are down globally, as consumer electronics prices skyrocket due to the ongoing memory shortage.

But just how much should a camera and smartphone mix? Consumers are showing strong interest in compact cameras and action cameras at a time when the smartphone in our pocket can capture better photos and videos than ever before. Perhaps there's a limit to how much one device can do. We'll have to wait and see if the Robot Phone becomes a real smartphone evolution, or a confusing amalgamation—remember Samsung's Galaxy Camera?

Updated August 12 at 11:30 am: This story has been updated with pricing information for the Honor Robot Phone.

entries.title: This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
entries.summary: Security researchers found that in less than 60 seconds, they could open a hatch on a plane’s exterior, plug in a tiny device, and redirect the aircraft’s autopilot or sabotage its flight plan.
entries.content:
Even as the digital components of so many life-critical systems have proven susceptible to cybersabotage—cars, medical devices, even water utilities and power grids—the computer systems of airplanes have, thankfully, remained uniquely inaccessible to hackers. But one group of academic researchers has spent years testing a different, devious approach to aviation cybersecurity. Perhaps, they suggest, a plane could be hacked the same way that spies and saboteurs have targeted other high-value, offline computers: by surreptitiously gaining physical access to one and plugging in a device designed to silently run the attackers' malicious code.

Tomorrow at the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference, researchers from the University of California at San Diego and Oberlin College will present a hacking technique capable of commandeering the autopilot of a Boeing 737 to redirect its navigation or silently altering key values in the plane's takeoff and fuel calculations while spoofing the results on the pilot's screen—subtle changes the researchers say could potentially cause anything from runway overruns on takeoff to diversions to a different country's airspace to catastrophic crashes.

To carry out that hacking, they've built a roughly coin-sized, Wi-Fi-enabled prototype device that costs less than $100. In less than a minute, that hardware implant can be fitted into a port accessible via a hatch on the exterior of the plane, one that's routinely within reach of maintenance workers or other airport and airline staff between flights. Once it's in place, the device can send electrical signals on one of the 737's internal networks to spoof commands to sensitive computer systems that guide its autopilot and show the pilot variables like the plane's total weight and outside air temperature, which play a critical role in a 737's takeoff calculations.

By proving the viability of that technique, the result of a process that stretched over more than a decade and entailed buying tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of plane components for testing, they hope to show that this sort of physical access hacking represents a practical threat in the hands of well-resourced saboteurs and a significant blind spot in aircraft security. Compared to the traditional threat of simply planting a bomb on a plane, they argue, it's also an approach that would offer an attacker more control, stealth, and deniability.

“If you could get 60 seconds with an airplane, what could you do?” asks Stefan Savage, one of the UCSD computer science professors who led the project, describing the question that first motivated their line of research. “Well, it turns out there’s a port that’s externally accessible. You can get to it with no special tools in about 15 seconds. And you can shove in a piece of electronics a little bigger than a quarter that lets you basically tell the autopilot what to do and lie to the pilot about changes to the flight plan.”

The researchers aren't revealing which port they targeted on the 737, nor are they releasing some details of how their hacking device is able to spoof commands to the plane's computers. They've worked closely with Boeing to share their findings, first disclosing elements of their research to the company more than six years ago, and going so far as to test out and demonstrate their attack in a Boeing facility's test lab.

When WIRED reached out to Boeing about the researchers' work, it responded in a statement that it had carried out its own review of its components' designs, installations, and interfaces in response to the researchers' findings. But it downplayed the practical risk of their physical-access hacking technique. “Our technical experts are confident that the layers of protection in place on the airplane, including within the system design and the operating environment, provide sufficient mitigation to significantly limit the feasibility and risk of real-world attacks,” the statement reads.

For their part, the researchers say, Boeing hasn't told them about any technical fix for the vulnerabilities they've discovered—and they speculate that the company may not in fact implement any such update to their systems for years to come, given how rarely commercial airplanes are redesigned.

That lack of an immediate security update for planes shouldn't be cause for panic or grounding aircraft, they write in their paper. “All of the authors of this paper routinely travel on Boeing 737 aircraft and expect to continue doing so,” the introduction of the paper reads.

Savage argues, though, that the research has demonstrated the need for long-term changes in both the cybersecurity of airplane components and, perhaps more immediately, the operational security measures that determine who can access a plane while it's on the ground. Their simplest fix suggestion: Plug the port with epoxy, or remove it altogether.

“This is something the aviation industry will want to plan to defend against,” Savage says. “I would not sleep on this one.”

Building a Plane, Then Breaking It

This particular team of researchers' interest in hacking a plane originated nearly a decade and a half ago, when some of them discovered and demonstrated the first successful over-the-internet techniques for hacking a car's computer systems, including its steering and brakes. Their proof-of-concept attack methods, particularly ones carried out by exploiting a Chevy Impala's OnStar system, launched an era of automotive hacking research that ultimately led to a sea change in carmakers' cybersecurity practices, including launching bug bounty programs for cars and hiring car hackers to help them root out vulnerabilities.

In the wake of that car-hacking work, one member of the team, then UCSD research scientist Kirill Levchenko, suggested they try hacking airplanes next. But unlike a Chevy Impala, a Boeing 737 was well beyond their budget. “I pointed out that we can’t exactly buy a plane and put it in the parking lot, but he was undeterred,” Savage says.

Over the following years, the team began buying computer components from that commercial aircraft whenever they could find them for sale, spending tens of thousands of dollars to acquire the equipment on the secondhand market. By 2019 they had assembled what they called Triton, an “avionics test bed" that essentially consisted of wired-together 737 computer parts.

Around the same time, UCSD professor Aaron Schulman was working on another research project on credit card skimmer devices that hackers were physically planting on gas station point-of-sale terminals to steal payment information. “We realized that it's a reasonable threat for someone to plug a device into a bus and read stuff off of it and potentially even gain control of it,” says Schulman, using the term “bus” to mean an internal network connecting components of a piece of digital equipment. Schulman began to wonder if a similar physical access attack might work on the internal bus of a plane. “We were like, ‘Wait a minute, we’ve got to rethink everything.’”

With that idea in mind, one of Schulman's then student researchers, Sam Crow, hunted through hundreds of pages of Boeing wiring diagrams and found that one particular port—typically protected by only a hatch without a lock—connected to a certain 737 bus that carries the data for two crucial computer components on the plane, its Flight Management Computer and its Multipurpose Control Display Unit. Soon after, Crow discovered, using the group's avionics test bed, that when he connected to that bus and sent electrical signals with a higher current than the legitimate ones used to send commands between those components of the 737, he could override those commands with his own, a technique that the researchers would later dub “Bus Driver.”

Now he had found an accessible foothold on the network from which he could send those electrical commands and tamper with the plane’s flight plan and critical parts of the pilot's interface. As Savage puts it, “it was like he had found the goddamn exhaust port on the Death Star.”

A Tiny Stowaway With In-Flight Wi-Fi

In the spring of 2020, the team alerted Boeing to its findings and got a surprisingly interested response. They would continue to share updates with the company on their findings for years to come.

Crow quickly refined their hacking device until he had a version of it that was small enough to fit into the exposed port on the 737 under a dust cap that typically covered it, entirely hiding the device from view. The tiny gadget included a chip capable of running their attack code as well as a Wi-Fi radio. That radio would, in theory, allow the hacking device to connect to the internet via the plane's in-flight Wi-Fi network and then beacon out to whoever controlled it, allowing the attacker to remotely control the device and the commands it sent.

When Covid hit, Schulman shipped the team’s avionics equipment to Crow’s Bay Area home, and he continued working on it in his bedroom. Soon he had improved their device's ability to imperceptibly intercept, alter, and spoof commands to the plane's sensitive systems: It could, for instance, connect to the Flight Management Computer and alter the waypoints programmed into the plane's autopilot, redirecting the plane's flight, or alter variables like its weight or the outside temperature. By electronically tampering with the Multipurpose Control Display Unit, meanwhile, it could prevent those changes from showing up on the pilot's screen.

Trick the pilot into thinking the outside air was colder—or the plane's load of passengers and cargo was lighter—than in reality, and the 737 might not achieve the necessary speed for takeoff before running out of runway. Mess with the flight plan, and you could cause the autopilot to change the plane's heading to make it enter another country's airspace, where it could be commandeered by that country's air force. A sudden navigation change could potentially crash a plane into a mountain, or a slow one could send a transoceanic flight in the wrong direction until it ran out of fuel over water. “It could be something as subtle as, you're in the Pacific, you see blue everywhere, and this diverts you 3 degrees off course, and now you're in the middle of nowhere,” Schulman says.

The researchers note that a careful pilot would be able to recover from almost any of the attacks they've imagined: Taking manual control of the plane overrides its autopilot, and even if the Multipurpose Control Display Unit were hacked, the correct values would show up on a different screen in the cockpit. But even in this scenario, Schulman says, the pilot “would see that this is not lining up, but they would have no idea why, and it would be very confusing and probably lead them toward an uncertain conclusion about what to do next.” In a less optimistic scenario—or if the hacker implements a more subtle change—Schulman says a pilot might not notice until it was too late.

In their paper, the researchers outline a range of fixes for the vulnerability they've uncovered, starting with removing the connector in the vulnerable port altogether, or plugging it with epoxy. More long-term, though, they suggest planes' systems could be updated to include defenses in their software that detect their Bus Driver hacking technique, or that better electrically isolate systems, as in some military aircraft, or even add cryptographic authentication to prevent spoofing of signals among the plane's systems.

Calling for these kinds of updates—not just for Boeing, but across the aviation industry—is far from alarmist given the practicality of the attack the researchers describe, says Beau Woods, a cybersecurity consultant who has served as an adviser to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and as a member of Boeing's Industry Cyber Technical Council. “It is entirely possible to have someone who is on staff go up to an airplane when it's on the ground, going through maintenance, and put this type of thing in there,” says Woods, who read the researchers' work ahead of publication. The paper, he says, “looks like solid empirical evidence about some realistic scenarios for high-capability adversaries.”

The researchers' technique, he says, shows how the “threat model” for any highly sensitive system has to change as potential attackers' technology advances—in this case, as it became possible to fit an entire hardware setup capable of connecting to a plane's Wi-Fi and relaying commands to its systems onto a tiny disc hidden inside the dust cap of an obscure plug.

“Now that the research has been published, it can be understood and recognized that the reality has changed,” Woods says. “Threat models from the 20th century rarely survive contact with 21st-century tools and techniques.”
